learningObjective: Explain why def-use chains are trivial to compute in SSA compared to non-SSA IR.
stem: In SSA form, why are def-use chains typically simpler and cheaper to compute than in a non-SSA IR?

options.text: Because SSA prohibits loops, def-use chains cannot cross backedges.
Because SSA merges phi values at runtime into a single memory slot, the def-use graph collapses to a linear list.
Because each SSA name has exactly one textual definition, every use points unambiguously to that unique def; there is no reaching-definitions problem to solve to associate uses with their defs.
Because SSA form guarantees that any use is reachable from every def, making the chains trivially total.

explanation: SSA guarantees a unique textual definition per name, so each use has a single unambiguous def. In non-SSA IR, reaching-definitions analysis is needed to determine which of possibly many textual definitions of a variable can reach a use. Options B, C, D contain incorrect claims about SSA semantics.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SSA supports loops (via loop-header phis).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SSA does not merge phi values into single memory slots; phi is an IR construct.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: unique-definition property makes def-use chains direct.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SSA doesn't guarantee every use is reachable from every def; each use has one unique reaching def.

nonImplications: Does not imply def-use chains are free to build in SSA; they still require a linear scan.
Does not imply non-SSA def-use analysis is infeasible; it just requires a dataflow analysis pass.
